job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: David Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at a payments company in Oslo. My day is code reviews, a standup at ten, and mostly fixing bugs in the part of the system that handles refunds. My final project at university in Bergen was a shift scheduler for a hospital ward, so I like practical software. I share a flat with two other people, and on weekends I go hiking or visit my grandmother, who still lives in the house where my dad grew up. I use an AI assistant for boring bits like tests, but I check everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected, helpful but not magic. At work we'd keep using it for tests and documentation. My team lead Silje would say we've got the same backlog as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. The refund system has rules, and rules mean someone has to understand them. I'd keep an eye on the market, since Oslo has lots of tech jobs but also plenty of graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and learning. I'd try to move from fixing bugs to building features within a year. I'd keep paying down nothing, because I have no debt, and I'd put a little into index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I think. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Oslo has plenty of graduates. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me at the moment, because I'm in. But I notice that the new people who join are better than I was a year ago. It reminds me that someone's always coming up behind you, with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving to features give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More say in what we build, and a better raise at review time. Silje says people who own a whole feature get noticed. I like that because refunds are not exciting, but they matter, and I'd like to work on something people notice.

say: It's **helpful but not magic**, and we'd use it for tests and documentation.
Silje would say we have the same backlog as before.
think: Refund rules need someone who understands them, so I feel **fine**.
Oslo has many jobs but also many **graduates** behind me.
do: Aim to move from bug fixing to building **features** within a year.
Put a little into **index funds**, since I have no debt.
S0.quote: Someone's always coming up behind you, with or without AI.
fieldNote: He is secure now, and the only pressure is **competition**.
He treats AI as a handy assistant and checks its output.
His career focus is on ownership of features.

steps.text: Take on one full refund feature this year
Put 400 a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll all have to work differently. I'd tell friends that the entry-level path is getting narrower. At work I'd say let's use the tools properly and write down what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the bug fixing I do now is what an AI does fastest. The company might need fewer juniors, and I'd need to prove that I'm worth more than a licence. The thing that would help me is understanding the business, not just the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools in every task, and I'd learn how the payment rules work, so I could review what the tools generate. I'd ask Silje to let me sit in on customer calls, which most developers avoid. And I'd keep a few months more in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, I'd say. But also curious, because it's like a new game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd need to prove you're worth more than a licence. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm the one who can say this refund rule comes from the bank's contract, and here's why, then I'm more useful than a tool that guesses. I'd want my name on the answer when something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why customer calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because most bugs come from not knowing what the customer meant. Developers like me tend to hide behind tickets, so a developer who actually talks to users is rarer. I'm a bit shy, so it would stretch me.

say: We'll all work differently, and the **entry-level path** is getting narrower.
I'd propose we use the tools properly and write down what works.
think: Bug fixing is what AI does fastest, so I must be worth more than a **licence**.
Knowing the business would help more than knowing code.
do: Use AI on every task and learn how the **payment rules** work.
Sit in on **customer calls**, which most developers avoid.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but curious, like a new game.
S1.quote: Developers like me tend to hide behind tickets, so a developer who actually talks to users is rarer.
fieldNote: He tries to climb **up the value chain** toward business knowledge.
His shyness is the real obstacle to his plan.
He treats AI adoption as a given.

steps.text: Use AI tools on every task and review the output carefully
Learn the bank contract rules behind refunds
Join customer calls once a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and no firm or government is ready. I'd tell friends to build some savings. At work I'd be honest, and ask Silje how she sees our team in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think developer jobs would be hit hard. A payments company can run with a handful of people if the AI writes and tests everything. I might be one of the handful or I might not. I can't tell, and that's the part that eats me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more money aside, maybe 60 percent of my pay. I'd look at roles that blend tech with people, like customer success or product. And I'd ask my parents, who live in Bergen, whether I could go back for a few months if I needed it, though I'd hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can tell myself I have savings, but I'd still check my bank balance more than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check your bank balance more than you should. What would you be looking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The number of months. I have about eight months of expenses, and watching that go to nine and ten makes me feel calmer. It's silly, but it's what I do when I'm worried. My dad does the same with his boat loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Silje?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm happy to do whatever the team needs, and I want to be someone she'd keep. She'd answer honestly, I think, but she'd also be waiting for the orders from above. So I'd end up with half an answer.

say: It's too fast, and no firm or government is **ready**.
At work I'd ask Silje how she sees our team in two years.
think: Developer jobs would be hit hard, and I can't tell if I'm one of the **handful** who stay.
The not knowing is what eats me.
do: Save about **60 percent** of my pay and watch the months in the bank.
Look at roles that blend tech and people, like **product** or customer success.
feel: I feel **anxious**, and I'd check my bank balance too often.
S2.quote: I can tell myself I have savings, but I'd still check my bank balance more than I should.
fieldNote: Eight months of savings and his parents' home keep him at **anxious**.
His coping habit is counting months of cushion.
He wants to move toward roles that machines reach later.

steps.text: Save 60 percent of my pay each month
Ask for a move into a product or customer success role
Ask my parents in Bergen if I can stay if I lose my job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a window. I'd tell friends to use it and not wait. At work I'd say we should train juniors differently, with more review and less typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect a squeeze around year three or four. By 2031 a lot of what I do is automated. I think I'd survive in a role like architect or team lead, if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year learning systems design and the payment domain properly. I'd go for a master's in the evenings, maybe in data and AI. I'd save for a flat deposit as well, since that stays valuable when jobs change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a master's, and not just learning on the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A degree still opens doors in Norway, and a master's would let me move to different companies or even the public sector. Also it's slower, which I like. I'd be learning properly, instead of racing the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want a flat. Why a flat in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when everything else is uncertain, a flat in Oslo is one thing that's physically there. My grandmother owns her house, and I've seen what that does for a person. She never worried about the market.

say: Five years gives us a window, so friends should **use it**.
I'd suggest training juniors with more review and less typing.
think: I expect a **squeeze** around year three or four, and by 2031 much of my work is automated.
I could survive as an architect or team lead if I start now.
do: Learn **systems design** and the payments domain in the first year.
Take an evening **master's** in data and AI and save for a flat.
feel: I feel **uneasy** more than anxious, and I like having a plan.
S3.quote: When everything else is uncertain, a flat in Oslo is one thing that's physically there.
fieldNote: He picks **slow, credentialed** moves over racing the tool.
The flat is his anchor, modelled on his grandmother's house.
He believes in planning rather than panic.

steps.text: Study systems design and payments rules in the first year
Start an evening master's in data and AI
Save 12,000 kroner a month for a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most people will adapt. At work I'd say we should keep adding skills, and I'd probably tell friends the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be 32 and in a different job. Maybe running a team or in a different field entirely. I'd worry more about my parents, who'd be near retirement, and how the system treats them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and buy that flat in about five years. I'd use AI tools like a normal part of the day. I'd look at moving into management or product in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is a bit like a long hike, you can pace yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mention your parents. What's the concern?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum is a nurse, and my dad is a harbour engineer. Their pensions are decent, but health care costs rise. If AI helps with that, great, but I can't be sure the savings reach people like them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pace yourself, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd review where I am every six months, like a checkpoint on a hike. If I'm learning, good. If I'm stuck, I'd change something small. It stops me panicking and stops me coasting.

say: Ten years is a long time and **most people will adapt**.
I'd tell friends to keep adding skills.
think: At 32 I'd be in a **different job**, maybe running a team.
I worry about my **parents'** health costs more than my own work.
do: Buy the **flat** in about five years and use AI as a normal tool.
Move toward **management** or product in year four.
feel: I feel **calm**, like pacing a long hike.
S4.quote: I'd review where I am every six months, like a checkpoint on a hike.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **calm**, and he plans reviews instead of fear.
His main worry is his **parents'** health care costs.
His hiking metaphor is a real habit.

steps.text: Buy a flat in about five years
Review my skills and options every six months
Look at a product management role in year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. Two years is too little for juniors to pivot, and companies won't wait. What would help is clear signals from employers about what skills they'll still pay for, some public retraining and a bit of time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as optimistic or as scared as people think my age should be. I'm somewhere in the middle, checking my bank balance and writing tests.

headlineQuote: Ten years is a bit like a long hike, you can pace yourself.
portrait: David is a **22-year-old** junior developer at a payments firm in Oslo, top of his class from Bergen.
He uses AI tools **now and then** and checks every result.
His outlook is centrist and practical, with a habit of **counting months** of savings.
He is calm with ten years, and **anxious** when two years leave no time to pivot.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, because juniors have no time to pivot.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **employer signals** on skills, public retraining and a little time.
